app.name: Storm Watch
app.description: A junior astronaut mission trainer where real NASA solar storm data sets the clock.
app.metaDescription: Storm Watch: a junior astronaut mission trainer where real NASA solar storm data sets the clock.
app.ogDescription: Command a Moon or Mars outpost for seven sols using real NASA solar storm data.
app.tagline: The real Sun sets the clock.

learn.air: Air machines need power every day.
learn.marsDelay: Mars messages take minutes. Crews there must decide alone.

quiz.title: Quick space check
quiz.shieldCosmic.question: What does your shelter shield block best?
quiz.shieldCosmic.explanation: Shields block storm particles well, not cosmic rays.
quiz.clockRisk.question: Why watch the Storm Clock closely?
quiz.clockRisk.explanation: Forecasts can be wrong, and waiting risks injury.
quiz.marsDelay.question: Why are Mars warnings harder than Moon warnings?
quiz.marsDelay.explanation: Radio signals take 3 to 22 minutes to Mars.
glossary.radiation.definition: Fast invisible energy moving through space.
glossary.solarFlare.definition: A bright flash of light from the Sun.
glossary.solarStorm.definition: A big burst of solar light and particles.
glossary.particles.definition: Tiny fast bits of matter that harm crews.
glossary.cosmicRays.definition: Steady high-energy rays from outside our solar system.
glossary.shield.definition: Thick walls that block solar storm particles.
glossary.sol.definition: One full day on a world.
glossary.radioDelay.definition: Time a signal needs to cross space.
glossary.twoStars.definition: Earn 8 science on the Moon, or 3 on Mars.
simplified.point1: Bolts, power, air, and health are game numbers, not NASA numbers.
simplified.point2: Storm damage is simplified, not a medical dose.
simplified.point3: Real particles can arrive earlier than the forecast.
simplified.point4: Forecast error range is a game choice, not NASA data.
simplified.point5: Flares are light. Fast particles harm crews.
simplified.point6: Big Mars storms rarely reach three stars.
teacher.title: Storm Watch: Ten-Minute Space Weather Lab
teacher.goal: Students compare solar storm choices on the Moon and Mars. Two stars need 8 science on the Moon, 3 on Mars.
teacher.bases: Moon: Entoto Base. Mars: Dallol Base.
teacher.activity1: Predict if particles will follow the flare.
teacher.activity2: Pick Moon Cadet with seed 101 and flare 2024-05-11.
teacher.activity3: Play seven sols and read the saver tip.
teacher.activity4: Collect the storm and compare mission results.
teacher.activity5: Fly the same storm on Mars with seed 101.
teacher.activity6: Compare sunlight, radio delay, and crew health.
teacher.activity7: Open Class challenge and record group results.
teacher.question1: Why could a shield not stop every daily health drop?
teacher.question2: When is working one more block worth the risk?
teacher.question3: How did Mars sunlight change your plan?
classroom.title: Classroom mode
teacher.learning1: Shields slow solar particles, not cosmic rays.
teacher.useCollection: Collect storms and compare real results.
info.sources.title: Where does this come from?
info.sources.intro: Storm events come from NASA DONKI FLR and SEP logs.
info.simplified.title: What is simplified?
info.glossary.title: Space Weather Glossary
info.about.title: About Storm Watch
info.about.team: Built by BuildLX for NASA Space Apps 2026.
info.about.data: Real storm data comes from NASA DONKI. Radiation facts come from NASA NTRS and NASA Science pages.
info.about.ai: AI coding tools helped write code and text. The builder reviewed and tested every file.
info.about.placeNames: Our names nod to Ethiopia’s Entoto and Dallol. Entoto has an observatory above Addis Ababa. Scientists study hot, colorful Dallol as Mars-like in Ethiopia’s Afar region.
info.about.branding: This game uses no NASA logos or branding. It is not an official NASA product.
fact.curiosity-rad-mars.text: Curiosity measured 0.7 mSv per day on Mars.
fact.curiosity-rad-cruise.text: On the trip to Mars, Curiosity measured 1.84 mSv per day.
fact.moon-radio-delay.text: Radio signals reach the Moon in about 1.3 seconds.
fact.mars-radio-delay.text: Radio signals to Mars take up to 22 minutes one way.
fact.mars-radio-delay-close.text: Mars radio delay is about 3 minutes at closest approach.
fact.mars-sunlight.text: Mars gets about 43 percent of Earth sunlight.
fact.shield-particles-vs-cosmic.text: Shelters stop storm particles well, but cosmic rays pass through.
saver.benefit.safe: The crew would have stayed safe.
saver.benefit.moreScience: You would have earned more science.
